title: Case-by-case → uniform: the small-n Bieberbach proofs were all different
connection: Before de Branges, each n (2–6) needed a different method; the uniform proof came from changing the statement (Milin's stronger conjecture). ES analogue: the repo's exponential families each needed bespoke windows; look for a stronger uniform statement (Milin-like) that implies all of them.
why: Suggests searching for the right stronger statement rather than more cases.
first_step: List the proved families (3·2^s+1, 7·4^s+9, 63·2^s+1, 4^s+k) and extract the common certificate mechanism; formulate a single conjecture implying all and test it on the open families.

title: Ultraproduct transfer between F_q[T]-ES and ℤ-ES statements
connection: Ax–Kochen: first-order statements true for F_p((t)) for almost all p transfer to Q_p for almost all p. ES over F_q[T] has proved variants; ES is first-order over (ℤ, +, ·) (∀n ∃x,y,z), but Ax–Kochen transfers statements about valued fields (ℚ_p vs F_p((t))), not about ℤ with positivity; identify which ES-adjacent statements are about local/valued-field structures (and hence transferable) — reviewer repair.
why: Clarifies precisely which ES-type statements a model-theoretic transfer could ever reach (and that the full statement likely cannot).
first_step: Formulate ES sub-statements with bounded quantifier complexity (e.g. 'a certificate with C dividing a fixed polynomial in p') and check whether they are decidable/transferable.

title: q→∞ failure (Thm 2.1) ↔ few numerators per prime (Luca–Pappalardi, Mond–Portier A₃(p))
connection: ES_q(A,P) fails for a proportion → 1 of P as q → ∞ with deg P fixed; over Z, Σ_{p≤x} A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³(up to loglog), so a typical p has only polylog numerators m with m/p a 3-term sum.
why: Both say 'numerator size vs denominator size' governs a phase transition; the Z regime m ≍ p^δ is the analogue of q→∞ and its failure would be the integer twin of Thm 2.1.
first_step: Read Mond–Portier 2201.11805 and check whether the proof shows A₃(p) is supported on m ≤ (log p)^C for most p — if so record the integer 'Thm 2.1'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Constant numerator 4 fails in char ≥ 5 because leading coefficients are 1,2,3 ↔ 'x > n/4' archimedean bound
connection: Prop 1.2: 4/P with monic denominators fails for every P in char ≥ 5 (sum of three monic reciprocals has leading coefficient 1,2,3). Over Z the analogue is the archimedean bound x ≥ n/4 that makes m ≥ 4 the first hard numerator.
why: It shows that '4 > 3' is the genuine source of hardness; the integer statement 'm ≤ 3 trivial, m = 4 hard' has an exact FF mirror, which supports using FF degree bookkeeping as a model of archimedean size.
first_step: Write the dictionary entry 'leading coefficient count ↔ number of terms ≥ numerator' and check whether k-term m/n with m ≤ k is trivial in both worlds (it is over Z: m/n = Σ 1/n).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: One numerator-2 term trivializes ES: 4/n = 2/((n+1)/2) + 1/M + 1/M, M = n(n+1)/2
connection: For odd n: 4/n − 4/(n+1) = 4/(n(n+1)) = 2/M = 1/M + 1/M with M = n(n+1)/2. So allowing a single term with numerator 2 (and a repeat) solves every odd n.
why: Boundary marker: the 'weighted ES' world with weight vector (2,1,1) is trivial; difficulty is entirely in the all-ones weight vector.
first_step: Record as a lemma; then explore weight vectors (1,1,1) vs (1,1,2) vs (1,2,3) for distinct denominators.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Elsholtz–Planitzer approximate parametrizations for k ≥ 4 unit fractions
connection: For sums of four and more unit fractions, Elsholtz–Planitzer use approximate parametrizations to count solutions. ES is the k = 3 case where exact parametrizations (Type I/II) exist.
why: Their counting lower bounds for k ≥ 4 may have a pointwise version at specific n; a 4-term pointwise result plus a merging step would be a new route.

connection: In periodic scheduling, three unit-time tasks with periods x, y, z have total density 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. ES ⇔ some such task system has density exactly 4/n. The pinwheel problem studies schedulability of density vectors (Kawamura recently proved the 5/6-density conjecture).
why: Mostly a restatement, but scheduling theory has combinatorial classification tools for unit-fraction density vectors (harmonic periods, folding).
first_step: Read Kawamura's density-threshold proof to see if exact-density perfectly periodic schedules with three tasks are characterized.

connection: Znám's problem asks for sets where each element properly divides the product of the others plus one; equivalent to Egyptian equations Σ 1/x_i + 1/Π x_i = 1. Existence for all k ≥ 5 is known (Sun Qi); k = 2..4 have none.
why: A family where small k fail and large k work via explicit constructions; ES with 3 terms is analogous to 'small k', and 4/5-term ES variants may behave like Znám k ≥ 5.

title: Representation of 1 by k unit fractions: Sylvester/Curtiss bound and maximal denominators
connection: The largest denominator in Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i = 1 is bounded doubly exponentially (Curtiss/Kellogg; Ambro–Barcau sharp bound for rationals). For ES the largest denominator is ≤ poly(n).

connection: 4/n = 1/x + Σ_{i} 1/q_i with q_i primes: sums of reciprocals of distinct primes rarely have small denominators (the denominator is the product). So the world is nearly empty — a rigidity lemma.

first_step: Prove: Σ 1/q_i over distinct primes q_i (not dividing n) cannot equal 4/n − 1/x unless the q_i divide x·n — then enumerate.

title: Two-unit-fraction remainder: ES as 'reduce to the solved two-term problem'
connection: a/b = 1/y + 1/z is completely understood: solvable iff b has a divisor pattern (a divisor d of b² ... with d ≡ −b mod a style). So ES(p) ⟺ ∃x: (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction, which is a divisor condition on p²x² ... concretely on (4x − p)-related integers.
why: This is the standard route to the divisor form, but phrasing it as 'the two-term problem with a free parameter x' invites tools from the two-term theory (e.g. counting representations of a/b by two unit fractions is a divisor-count of b² in classes).

why: The theorem exhibits infinitely many extreme reciprocal configurations; its construction may be tested for generating thin families of ES-solvable primes.
first_step: Take the explicit infinite family in the proof and substitute its parameter into the ES certificate identity, checking whether a prime subfamily emerges.

title: Problem 300: reciprocal sum-set method and bounded length
connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F04, F12, F33: rich reciprocal sumsets and fixed-length additive-multiplicative structure.
why: The sumset methods behind density results may yield a structured subset of three-term sums even if unrestricted representations are plentiful.
first_step: Inspect the proof for sumset iteration; stop at the first stage producing three distinct reciprocals and test the resulting target set against primes 4/p.

title: Problem 304: greedy residual and split-hyperbola completion
connection: Problem 304 ↔ ES F12, F15, F32: reciprocal expansion and fixed-denominator divisor fiber.
why: After a greedy first term, ES completion is a divisor equation; denominator bounds from 304 may make that fiber search sharply finite.
first_step: Choose x=floor(p/4)+1 in 4/p, derive the residual two-term equation, and compare its divisor parameter with bounds used in 304.

title: Problem 302: density threshold as a quantitative toy model
connection: Problem 302 ↔ ES F01, F05, F12, F24: forced reciprocal solution above density threshold versus ES heuristic existence.
why: An explicit threshold in a nearby reciprocal equation offers a tractable toy model for converting witness-density heuristics into a theorem.
first_step: Work through the simplest density estimate on the page and compare its combinatorial lower bound with a numerical estimate of ES candidate triples at primes.

title: The largest exceptional denominator as a function of numerator
connection: For Schinzel's k/n variant, the MO question asks for the largest failure n(k), and notes a lower-growth bound. This shares F11/F12/F24/F25: numerator threshold, fixed number of unit fractions, heuristic finite exceptions, and explicit small failures.
why: A scaling law for n(k) could distinguish genuinely special features of 4/n from generic Egyptian-fraction existence.
first_step: For several small k, exhaustively find all n up to a modest cutoff with no three-term decomposition and plot the maximum against k; compare with the k^(8/7) growth suggested in the MO question and with Pomerance–Weingartner's proven lower bound n_k ≥ exp(k^{1/3+o(1)}) (arXiv:2511.16817).

title: Pierce expansions: alternating unit-fraction dynamics
connection: Pierce expansions share F12,F16w,F27,F32: rational numbers are encoded by a finite sequence of integer choices and positive unit-fraction arithmetic. ES asks for a fixed-term positive representation rather than a variable-length expansion.
why: The recurrence may expose transformations between neighboring denominators or a stopping criterion tied to congruence classes.
first_step: Write the Pierce recurrence for 4/p and check whether a two-step truncation yields a three-term ES certificate for any residue classes.

title: Liu–Sawhney further unit-fraction questions (Erdős problems)
connection: Liu–Sawhney (2024) resolve several Erdős–Graham unit-fraction questions with refinements of Bloom's method; ES is a fixed-length unit-fraction problem.
why: Most transferable pieces: control of unit-fraction sums over smooth numbers with prescribed denominators.
first_step: Read Liu–Sawhney and list each lemma that works for a fixed small number of terms.
refs: Liu–Sawhney, On further questions regarding unit fractions, arXiv:2404.07113

title: Term-count calibration: Vose / Tenenbaum–Yokota bounds on the number of unit fractions needed
connection: Every a/b is a sum of O(√log b) distinct unit fractions (Vose), with refined bounds by Tenenbaum–Yokota. ES fixes the numerator 4 and asks for exactly 3 terms. The term-count axis is a native calibration of Egyptian-fraction methods.
why: It locates where existence becomes easy (k growing slowly) and shows that ES sits at the extreme small-k end.
first_step: Collect the known results for fixed numerator a and k terms (a = 4: k = 3 open; for k ≥ 4 trivial with repetition); check whether 'distinct denominators, k = 4' for 4/n is proved for all n.
refs: Tenenbaum–Yokota, Length and denominators of Egyptian fractions (JNT 1990)

title: Covering-system disproof search on exponential families (Sierpiński-type)
connection: Sierpiński/Erdős obstructions arise when every member of an exponential family is forced to have a small prime factor. For ES families n_s = k·2^s + 1, check whether a covering system could force every certificate condition to fail for all s (it would give infinitely many ES counterexamples).
why: Disproof-side: open families (15·2^s + 1, 4^s + 297) are exactly where such an obstruction would show up first.
first_step: For n_s = 15·2^s + 1, compute for small (C, d) the periodic sets of s with a certificate; check whether their union is all s (proof) or misses a progression (potential covering obstruction).
refs: Erdos, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950) 113-123 (On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems)

title: Average over p of Schinzel-type events for the polynomials 4Cp + 1 in C
connection: Skorobogatov–Sofos average over polynomial families. At fixed p, the family {4Cp + 1 : C} is a linear polynomial in C; averaging over p (with C free) gives Schinzel-on-average-type statements on factorisations of 4Cp + 1 that underlie the almost-all ES theorem. Make explicit which 'Schinzel on average' input the almost-all proof uses and whether a pointwise-in-p version is a known open problem.
why: Locates ES exactly within the Schinzel-on-average landscape (what is averaged, over what).
first_step: Rewrite Vaughan's almost-all proof as a statement about factorisations of 4Cp + 1 averaged over p; identify the pointwise analogue.
refs: arXiv:2005.02998 (Skorobogatov-Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points)

title: Archimedean crux restated as a 'gap principle' in valuation theory
connection: Cones discrete at all places where they carry sign (ℕ, monic F_q[T], Gaussian sector) give lottery problems; non-discrete cones collapse. Formalize: ES over (R, C) is a finite covering problem iff C ∩ {|x|_v < 1} ≠ ∅ for some sign place v.
why: A precise theorem of this kind would classify all analogue worlds at once and certify that Z is in the hard class.
first_step: State the theorem for Dedekind domains with a cone given by sign conditions at finitely many places; prove the 'collapse' direction from Lemma 3.1.

title: Integer ES solutions with x = Tr, y·z from norms: 'quadratic orbit' ES
connection: Variant: two denominators conjugate in a real quadratic field (y, ȳ) and one rational x: 4/n − 1/x = Tr(y)/N(y). Then (for solutions where y, z are conjugate quadratic integers) 4/n − 1/x = Tr(y)/N(y): a condition that (numerator, denominator) of 4/n − 1/x arise as (trace, norm) up to scaling — a binary quadratic form condition. (Requiring Tr(y) | N(y) would collapse to the two-term problem, which fails e.g. at n = 5.)
why: Converts ES into representation of numbers by binary quadratic forms with a trace constraint, linking to genus theory and class numbers (repo's CLASS_FORCING).
first_step: Make the equivalence explicit: 1/y + 1/ȳ = (y+ȳ)/(yȳ); classify which (t, N) arise and derive the binary-form condition.

title: ES over Z[i] for Gaussian primes in the sector cone: does the T1 square obstruction appear at Gaussian squares?
connection: If a Gaussian analogue of certificate lines exists, T1 predicts emptiness at Gaussian squares π² with suitable congruence. Test whether Gaussian squares are the hardest Gaussian-cone cases.
why: A T1 analogue in Z[i] would show T1 is about quadratic reciprocity in general number fields (quartic reciprocity may refine it).
first_step: Classify Gaussian-cone solutions by type and check emptiness of 'line' families at π² for small π.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: 'Some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fails at exactly the same primes 17, 241 as m = 8
connection: Among p < 4000 the solutions with a denominator divisible by 4 are missing exactly at p = 17 and 241, the same primes where 8/p fails. A structural equivalence (e.g. a bijection of solution types) may lie behind this.
why: If 'a denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' ⇔ '8/p three-term' (up to finitely many cases), ES's 2-adic structure (the I3 coordinate in 4Z ∪ (8Z − p)) gets a clean numerator interpretation.
first_step: Failure sets coincide (= {17, 241}) up to 2·10^4 as well (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Try to prove: if 4 | x in 4/p = Σ 1/x_i, then a solution of 8/p can be produced (and conversely).
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0195] Case study of 4/241: list its 8 solutions (all have a multiple of 3, none a multiple of 4) and relate to 241 ≡ 1 (mod 240).
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)

title: Idoneal numbers and ES: non-representability by xy + yz + zx is tied to class groups of discriminant −4N (check the exact criterion)
connection: Euler's idoneal numbers are those with one class per genus (class group elementary 2-abelian); Borwein–Choi relate non-representability by xy+yz+zx to such class-group conditions, but the equivalence is not literal (e.g. N = 3 = 1+1+1 is represented although h(−12) = 1), so the exact criterion must be read off their paper. ES might be reformulated as a statement about elements of order > 2 in class groups of discriminants tied to p.
why: A 'class group has an element of order ≥ 3 with property X' statement is the kind of thing known for all large discriminants (Weinberger, under GRH); an ES statement of that type would make ES GRH-conditional.
first_step: Derive, from an ES solution, a binary form of discriminant −4N (N = 4xyz/p) and identify its class; test whether non-2-torsion is forced.
refs: Borwein–Choi, 'On the representations of xy+yz+zx', Experiment. Math. 9 (2000)

title: Ternary quadratic forms (Duke–Schulze-Pillot): local ⇒ global except spinor exceptions ↔ T1
connection: Large integers locally represented by a positive ternary form are represented, except finitely many spinor square classes (ineffective via Siegel). T1 at odd squares is ES's analogue of a spinor exception: a square-class phenomenon that blocks a uniform method but not the truth.
why: If ES certificates can be encoded as representations by a family of ternary forms, Duke–Schulze-Pillot gives 'all large p' ineffectively, with T1 as the spinor exception.
first_step: Read THREE_SQUARES.md / z31_quadratic_forms.md for prior attempts; check whether some ES slice is exactly a ternary representation problem.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0035] Check whether T1 can be read as a spinor-exception phenomenon for an attached ternary quadratic form (QUATERNION_ES.md).
[signature-0033] Locate in QUATERNION_ES which ternary form's representations map to ES witnesses; compute its theta series coefficient size at primes.
[signature-0114] Read the theorem's spinor-exception square-class condition and test whether ES's failed certificate subfamilies can be organized into analogous square classes.

title: Artin's primitive root conjecture (Hooley under GRH) ↔ 'some ℓ has 1+ℓ^k with a 3 mod 4 factor'
connection: The Z[1/ℓ] mechanism needs η = ℓ^k with ℓ^k ≡ −1 mod e for some e ≡ 3 mod 4: an order condition on ℓ modulo e. Hooley-type GRH arguments control such order conditions for almost all ℓ.
why: Formally parallel to Artin; but our Zsigmondy item suggests an unconditional proof for all ℓ is easy. Use as a sanity link.
first_step: Prove unconditionally via the reciprocity argument (failure forces ℓ ≡ 1 mod 8) plus a choice of k; no GRH needed.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: p-dependent field Q(√p): N(ε_p) = −1 for p ≡ 1 mod 4, so positive ES over O_{Q(√p)} holds for 4/p
connection: For prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 the fundamental unit of Q(√p) has norm −1 (classical), so Prop 3.3 applies in K_p = Q(√p) itself, where p = (√p)² ramifies. The ES-solving unit η = ε_p^{2j} now depends on p.
why: This is the first 'proved world attached to p': trace/norm descent from K_p to Q would give a p-dependent integer identity (numerator 8 via traces), i.e. an integer statement whose ingredients are Pell solutions of x² − p y² = −1.
first_step: For p ≤ 200 compute ε_p, the inert prime ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 and η ≡ −1 mod ℓ, write the K_p solution of 4/p, and compute its trace-descent (8/p = Σ Tr/N) to see if denominators ever become unit fractions.

title: Repeated denominators never occur for p ≡ 1 (mod 4): explains 'distinct is WLOG'
connection: The data (499/499 primes) show no solution with x = y or y = z. Proof sketch: x = y gives z = px/(2(2x − p)); gcd(2x − p, x) | p forces 2x − p ∈ {1, p}, and 2x − p = 1 needs x = (p+1)/2 even, i.e. p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Similar for y = z.
why: A clean lemma removing a case and showing the 'repeat world' is empty exactly in the hard class — another archimedean/2-adic coincidence.
first_step: Write out both cases (x = y, y = z) carefully and record the lemma.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quaternion ES with norm constraint: N(x) fixed forces x into finitely many points — 'quaternion slices'
connection: In a definite quaternion order, elements of norm m are finite (r₄(m) of them). Requiring 1/x = x̄/N(x) with N(x) | stuff gives finitely many options per norm: quaternion ES is a union of finite slices indexed by norms, like ES's e-slices.
why: The count r₄(m) is a modular form coefficient (Jacobi four squares), so quaternion ES slice counts are modular — a possible source of exact formulas.
first_step: Write the quaternion ES slice count as a sum of r₄-type coefficients; compare to QUATERNION_ES.md.

title: Tropical-at-p world: Type I vs Type II as the two cells of the p-adic tropicalization
connection: At the target prime p, v_p of (x, y, z) must satisfy the tropical equation: min valuation of 4xyz vs of p(xy + yz + zx). The tropical picture alone also allows the cell where all three denominators are divisible by p (locally e.g. x = y = z = 3p/4); globally that cell is excluded only by positivity (4/p = (1/p)Σ1/a_i would need Σ 1/a_i = 4 > 3). So Type I/II completeness = tropical cells + archimedean positivity.
why: Shows which part of the Type I/II split is local and which is archimedean, and suggests analogous splits at ℓ = 2 (the 2-adic cells explain the m = 8 / 4 | denominator observations).
first_step: Write the 2-adic tropical cells and match them to the 2-adic constraint-world data (all even, 4 | denominator).

title: Gaussian twin of the e-slice: e = 1/u + 1/v in the Gaussian cone — are there more universal e?
connection: Over Z only e ∈ {1, 2}. In the Gaussian cone, 1/u + 1/v can be other Gaussian integers (e.g. with u, v conjugate-ish), giving extra universal divisors and possibly covering more classes mod 4Z[i].
why: If the Gaussian cone has a richer universal-e set, its open conjecture may be 'closer to finite covering' than ES — and the extra e's show exactly what Z lacks.
first_step: Enumerate Gaussian e in the cone with e = 1/u + 1/v, u, v in the cone and small norm; classify residues mod 4.

title: Heath-Brown's one-of-three primitive-root theorem
connection: A pointwise family of three candidate bases guarantees that at least one succeeds infinitely often; this is an infinite-family covering result (F34) rather than a single-input universal theorem. It offers a contrasting way to combine several incomplete witness families (F08,F34).
why: ES has many certificate lines each covering thin prime sets; the theorem's finite-family combination strategy is worth testing for analogous line families.
first_step: Identify the exact three-base linear sieve lemma in Heath-Brown and see if ES certificate-line sets have a comparable pairwise independence property.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0204] Find three ES families whose failure sets intersect only in primes with a special multiplicative structure; test numerically intersection of failures for pairs/triples of small-(a,d) families.
[signature-0023] Formulate the ES analogue 'for any three fixed (u,B) pairs, at most two lines fail for a positive proportion of p' — check it is trivial or false.
[tools-0228] List repo forcing lines and check whether any three are 'independent' in the sense needed for a Heath-Brown-type dichotomy.
refs: Heath-Brown, Artin's conjecture for primitive roots, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986)

title: U(p) residual is driven by L(1,χ_p) (Spearman −0.69)
connection: At ≈9 000 primes p≡1(4) <2·10⁵, the residual of log U(p) (after log p, loglog p) has Spearman ρ = −0.69 with L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p)·log ε_p/√p (real quadratic field Q(√p)); more small QRs ⇒ fewer solutions.
why: Gives a concrete arithmetic 'explanatory variable' for the ES count; the BM main term T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) (FRONTIER §2.2) is a weighted sum of the same character, so this is the data face of BM.
first_step: Prove/derive the expected-count heuristic E U(p) ≈ c(log p)² · F(χ_p) with F a finite Euler product, and compare F with our fitted exponent (−0.30).

title: At odd n, every solution has at least two even denominators
connection: Exactly-0-even and exactly-1-even solutions never occur at primes (2-adic parity: three odd unit fractions sum to odd/odd; one even denominator gives odd numerator over even); shares: 2 even 52%, all even 48%.
why: Trivial 2-adic lemma but a useful normal form: write x = 2x₁ or the pair y, z even; reduces 2-adic case analysis in parametrisations.
first_step: None beyond writing down the lemma.

title: Composite failures for 'none of x, y, z divisible by 4': exactly multiples of 16
connection: Among n ≤ 3000 the n with no ES solution having 4 ∤ x, 4 ∤ y, 4 ∤ z are 16, 32, 48, …; the analogous condition for 8 fails exactly at multiples of 32, for 9 at multiples of 9, for 5 at multiples of 5.
why: Clean local lemmas (p-adic valuation of n forces valuations of denominators); sanity checks for the variant engine.
first_step: Prove: v₂(n) ≥ 4 ⇒ 4 | some denominator; v₃(n) ≥ 2 ⇒ 9 | some denominator.

title: Discriminant squares
connection: After fixing one symmetric parameter, require the remaining quadratic discriminant to be square; compare with Pell-type searches.
why: Square conditions can package an infinite family more economically than individual divisors.
first_step: Derive the discriminant after prescribing y+z and x, then identify when a Pell equation appears.

title: Tropical balance regimes
connection: Separate the cleared equation into regimes according to which of xy,xz,yz dominate, using tropical-style bookkeeping.
why: Dominant balances may suggest complementary denominator ansatzes, not replace exact arithmetic.
first_step: List possible valuation balances at a prime dividing one denominator and derive the corresponding exact divisibility cases.

title: Pell families from denominator gaps
connection: Prescribe an affine relation between two denominators and ask when the resulting square condition yields a Pell family.
why: An infinite family of certificates could arise from a recurrent rather than polynomial parametrization.
first_step: Test y=z−h with h in 1 through 20 and classify the resulting discriminant equations.

title: Reciprocity as a design constraint
connection: Rather than discard square-like obstructions, use quadratic reciprocity to choose parameters with deliberately opposite symbols.
why: Symbols can guide which certificate family is worth trying at each prime.
first_step: For a small family, derive the Legendre-symbol necessary conditions and search complementary parameter choices.

title: p-adic denominator balance
connection: Classify valuations of x,y,z at p using the cleared equation and compare branches of the classification.
why: The valuation constraints are exact and can reduce redundancy in parametrizations.
first_step: Derive all possible minimum-valuation patterns before searching examples for each pattern.

title: Reciprocity-induced correlation
connection: Track how reciprocity couples residue information about p and its auxiliary factors.
why: Treating those symbols as independent would obscure exact constraints that might guide construction.
first_step: Tabulate both directions of Legendre symbols for successful certificates and derive the forced sign relation.

title: Petri nets for denominator resources
connection: Model valuation transfers under exact identity moves as token transitions between denominator components.
why: Conservation laws in the net may reveal which transformations can or cannot connect two families.
first_step: Derive a token transition from one exact move and compute its linear invariants.

title: S-unit support restrictions
connection: Fix a small set of allowed denominator primes and translate the reciprocal equation into an S-unit-type relation.
why: Restricted support gives a sharply defined subproblem whose solutions can be explored exactly.
first_step: For S={2,3,5,p}, enumerate bounded exponent triples and write the resulting multiplicative relations.

title: Local-to-global comparison in a fixed slice
connection: Compare exact integer representations with solvability modulo increasing moduli for one explicitly derived quadratic subproblem.
why: A discrepancy identifies what extra arithmetic data the slice requires while leaving other families untouched.
first_step: For a small form and target range, enumerate representations and modular solutions with a common documented bound.

title: Aharonov–Bohm phase / holonomy around the odd-square obstruction
connection: T1 says certificate lines are empty at odd squares for a reciprocity reason. A 'holonomy' interpretation: going around the square locus in the (p, C) parameter plane picks up a sign (Jacobi symbol). Mechanisms with nontrivial holonomy are forced to fail at squares — which is exactly what the barrier demands of any proof.
why: Reformulating T1 as a topological phase might guide the design of a mechanism that *provably* has the right failure mode at squares.
first_step: Write the Jacobi symbol (−C/p)-type sign that vanishes/flips at squares as a function on the parameter plane; check whether it is the Brauer class of Bright–Loughran evaluated at the fibre.

title: Z₂ gauge theory on the prime-factor hypergraph of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Each C gives a set of primes; a sign assignment (Legendre symbol (q/·)) on primes is a Z₂ gauge field; ES requires a 'Wilson loop' (product of symbols) to equal a target at some C. Gauge-invariant content = the frustration pattern.
why: Gauge-theoretic language can isolate what is invariant under rechoosing C; T1 (squares) is manifestly gauge-invariant.
first_step: Write the product of Legendre symbols Π (−p/q) over q | 4Cp+1 and relate to the divisor-class condition via reciprocity; check whether a known 'reciprocity sign' identity makes the product identically computable.

title: Conformal-field-theory c=1 / Gaussian free field model of Dedekind sums tied to 4/p
connection: Dedekind sums s(a,c) satisfy reciprocity and are governed by continued fractions; continued-fraction length λ(p) ≤ 3 (ES₅) might be expressible through Dedekind-sum identities (Rademacher's 3-term reciprocity).
why: Rademacher's three-term Dedekind reciprocity is exactly a 'three-term' relation — a formal resemblance to three unit fractions worth 30 minutes.
first_step: Write the ES₅ rational, compute its Dedekind sum, and test numerically whether ES solutions correspond to triples (a,b,c) in Rademacher's identity s(a,b)+s(b,c)+s(c,a) = ... with a 1/12-type constant involving 4/p.
refs: Rademacher, 'Generalization of the reciprocity formula for Dedekind sums' (1954)

title: Binary quadratic forms: Type I as representation of p² by a form of discriminant −16c²d
connection: f | p² + 4c²d means p² + 4c²d = f·g; representation theory of binary quadratic forms (Gauss composition) describes which f occur as 'first coefficients' of forms representing p² + 4c²d... Equivalently, (p, c·2√(−d)) is a vector in an imaginary quadratic order; the norm factorisation is governed by the class group of ℚ(√−d).
why: Class-group structure of ℤ[√−d] is *rigid* and the 'divisor in a residue class' condition on f may translate into a *genus* condition (which is a character condition, computable), leaving the class-group part.
first_step: Write the Type I condition in the order O_d = ℤ[2c√−d]: f is the norm of an ideal dividing (p + 2c√−d)? Check: N(p + 2c√−d) = p² + 4c²d. So f | N(α) for α = p + 2c√−d; ideal divisors of (α) have norms f; the residue condition f ≡ −p mod 4cd is a condition on the ideal class modulo 4cd (ray class group). Verify this translation numerically.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Primes p for which 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1, … are all 'sums of two squares type': structure of the joint exceptional set
connection: Following the C=1 criterion: the failure set for C ≤ K is {p : for every C ≤ K, 4Cp + 1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C}. For C with 4C having few residue classes ≡ −1 the condition is 'all prime factors in a subgroup' — a multiplicative-structure condition (like 'n is a norm from ℚ(i)').
why: Norm-type sets have Dirichlet-series descriptions (Landau), so the joint failure set for C ≤ K has a computable density ~ Π_C (1 − something)^(…) and a *structure* (a norm from a compositum?). If the joint failure set for all C were provably empty by a norm argument… that's ES. But at least the per-C structure is exact.
first_step: For C = 1,2,3: characterise 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' exactly in terms of prime factorisation (subgroup H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× not containing −1 and all factors in H_C? Not quite — subset products must avoid −1, which for a subgroup H ∌ −1 means all factors in H; else more complex). Tabulate for C ≤ 10.

title: Reciprocity proof of T1 as a *template*: what is the exact Jacobi-symbol identity, and does its negation at non-squares produce a divisor?
connection: T1's proof: if m² = (ab − 1)/(4C) with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C then ... a Jacobi symbol contradiction. At a non-square p, the same Jacobi symbol computation gives no contradiction but gives *information* — e.g., a constraint on (−C/p) or (p/a) that must hold for any certificate; this constraint is a 'necessary condition' on winning C, and might be the thing to make sufficient.
why: Necessary conditions on winning C from reciprocity (e.g. 'C must satisfy (−C/p) = +1'?) halve the search space; verify whether such a condition is known and whether data confirms it.
first_step: Derive: from 4Cp + 1 = ab, a ≡ −1 mod 4C: compute (a/p)·(b/p) = (ab/p) = (1/p) = 1, and (p/a) via reciprocity... obtain a condition on C mod p or (C/p). Test numerically which Jacobi symbols are forced for winning (C, a).

title: Kronecker's limit formula / class number h(−4d) as the 'main term' for Type I at fixed d
connection: Σ_c #{f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (4cd)} over c ≤ X is a sum over representations by forms of discriminant −16d... whose total is controlled by class numbers; Kronecker–Hurwitz-type formulas give Σ_c r_Q(p² + 4c²d) in terms of h(−d·) and L(1, χ).
why: Exact class-number formulas are 'rigid' inputs; if the Type I count at fixed d has a class-number main term with an explicit error, choosing d with large h(−4d)/√d (many classes, small discriminant) maximises the main term.
first_step: For d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 7} compute the Type I count over c ≤ X numerically for p ≈ 10⁶ and compare with h(−4d)·log X·const; estimate the constant.

title: Per-C exact sign structure: #{d | N, d ≡ −1 (m)} as a combination of multiplicative functions — the explicit product formula
connection: For m = 4C, #{d | N : d ≡ r (m)} = (1/φ(m)) Σ_χ χ̄(r) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). For N = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1 mod m the trivial character contributes τ(N)/φ(m); each nontrivial χ contributes χ̄(−1)·Π(...). ES(p) fails at C iff these cancel exactly to 0. 'Exact cancellation of a sum of φ(m) products' is a strong algebraic condition.
why: The exact-cancellation view suggests an algebraic-number-theoretic approach: the sum is an algebraic integer in ℚ(ζ_{φ(m)})… no, it's rational; but the Π over characters is a norm-like expression. Cancellation to 0 might be ruled out by a *valuation* argument (2-adic valuation of τ(N)/φ(m) vs the rest) for suitable C — a rigidity mechanism!
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation of the trivial-character term τ(N)/φ(4C) and of the sum of nontrivial terms for failing (p, C); check whether failures require specific 2-adic coincidences; if a C with v₂-mismatch always exists, that's a proof direction.

title: Cyclotomic rigidity directly: primes dividing Φ_m(x) are ≡ 1 mod m (or divide m). Find x, m with Φ_m(x) = 4Cp+1 and m | ... so that divisors ≡ 1 mod m; need ≡ −1 mod 4C though — use Φ_{2m} or the factor structure of x^m + 1
connection: Prime divisors q of x^m + 1 (odd m) satisfy q ≡ 1 mod 2m or q | 2(x+1)... more precisely primitive divisors of x^{2m} − 1 are ≡ 1 mod 2m. To get divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C we need a different rigidity: primes dividing x² + 1 are ≡ 1 mod 4 (wrong sign); primes dividing x² − 2 are ≡ ±1 mod 8; primes dividing x² + 2 are ≡ 1, 3 mod 8 — the '3 mod 8' is ≡ −1 mod 4 but not −1 mod 8. In general, primes dividing a binary form of discriminant D lie in classes determined by (D/q) = 1 — a *set* of classes, never a single class −1 mod 4C unless the genus theory is trivial. So cyclotomic/quadratic-form rigidity gives 'divisors in a SUBGROUP', not in a coset — and −1 mod 4C must be IN that subgroup. For 4C = 8: the subgroup {1,3} mod 8 (from x² + 2) contains 3 ≢ −1; {1,7} (from x² − 2) contains 7 ≡ −1 ✓. So: if 4Cp + 1 = x² − 2 for some x, then every prime factor is ≡ ±1 mod 8, and the product... need a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8 — exists iff some prime factor is ≡ 7 mod 8 (else all ≡ 1). Not forced. Conclusion: quadratic-form rigidity gives subgroup membership, not coset hitting. Record as a structured negative with the one escape: forms whose 'divisor subgroup' is exactly {±1} mod 4C make the problem a parity question.
why: Pinning down that classical rigidity (cyclotomic/quadratic) gives subgroups not cosets, and identifying the parity escape, is a reusable lemma for the 'generator matrix'.
first_step: Write the lemma; then search for binary forms Q with divisor subgroup {±1} ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× for small C (requires (ℤ/4C)^× to have a large... only C = 1 or 2 work, since index must be φ(4C)/2 for a quadratic form's genus… no: the subgroup of 'split primes' for ℚ(√D) has index 2; {±1} has index φ(4C)/2; equal only if φ(4C) = 4, i.e. 4C ∈ {8, 12}: C = 2, 3). So for C = 2: x² − 2 (divisors ≡ ±1 mod 8); C = 3: x² + 3 (divisors ≡ 1 mod 3 — hmm need ±1 mod 12: primes dividing x² + 3 are ≡ 1 mod 3 i.e. ≡ 1, 7 mod 12 — wrong). Tabulate properly.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0106] Search for algebraic identities 4Cp + 1 = A·B with A ≡ −1 mod 4C forced by cyclotomic structure when p has a special form (p = Φ_m(t)?).
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Euler–Goldbach: 4xy − x − y is never a square — T1 at level t = 4 is an 18th-century theorem
connection: The classical result (z² = 4xy − x − y has no positive solutions; MathOverflow 364853 traces origin and variations) is exactly the C = 1 case of T1 (D⁻₄(4m²+1) = 0). Shares F08 (square obstruction by reciprocity), F16.
why: The MO thread collects variations (other coefficients, more variables); each proved variation is a candidate new T1-type certificate or a candidate NON-obstruction, which is what ES needs at non-square n.
first_step: Read MO 364853 and its references; list every proved variant 'k·xy − x − y ≠ f(z)' and test which correspond to ES slices.

title: Borwein–Choi on idoneal numbers and three-variable factorization
connection: The equation n=xy+yz+zx is a three-variable bilinear representation with divisor parametrizations (F10,F16w), and the idoneal-number result is pointwise with at most a possible exceptional value under hypotheses (F01,F21).
why: Its class-group analysis of a universal representation problem could inform ES's divisor-sum count and its genus-character main term (F20).
first_step: Read the exact Borwein–Choi theorem and isolate how class-group characters bound the exceptional discriminant; compare the genus term with R(p)'s real-character term.
refs: J. M. Borwein, K.-K. S. Choi, On the representations of xy+yz+zx, Experiment. Math. 9 (2000) 153–158

title: Character orthogonality and real-character main terms
connection: Quadratic-form representation counts split into genus characters and an analytic remainder (F20,F31); ES likewise has a real-character main term in its sum over moduli (F20).
why: The decomposition may help isolate whether a genus-style positive main term can dominate the ES error for each prime, not merely on average.
first_step: For each C in R(p), expand the residue indicator using characters modulo 4C and explicitly separate principal, real, and nonreal characters for p≡1 mod 4.

title: Ternary lattice-coset representation versus ES three denominators
connection: Arxiv:2104.08798 treats ternary integral quadratic forms with congruence conditions, matching ES F12/F27/F31 and F03: three variables, positivity/integrality constraints, and congruence-restricted representations.
why: A ternary-form reduction could convert ES into a standard representation problem with mature local and spinor-genus tools.
first_step: Attempt the encoding for p≡1 mod 4 and verify whether the congruence conditions define a fixed lattice coset amenable to spinor-genus tests.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0205] Attempt to eliminate one ES denominator using a fixed slice and identify whether the remaining condition is a ternary quadratic form on a fixed coset.

title: Least nonresidue bounds as a reciprocity-search analogue
connection: The Fourier-optimization bounds for least quadratic nonresidues in arXiv:2404.08380 match ES F08/F29/F36 and F21: a pointwise quadratic-character condition is central, but conditional distribution bounds do not automatically solve a single-integer witness problem.
why: The technique is a specific character-sum optimization tool to compare with ES's reciprocity obstruction at squares.
first_step: Read the Fourier optimization setup and test whether its majorant/minorant can bound the number of ES parameters excluded by the relevant quadratic character.

title: Zhi-Wei Sun's family of refined-Lagrange conjectures with explicit finite exception lists
connection: Sun posed dozens of 'every n is … with constraint …' conjectures, each with finite explicit exceptions; several were proved (ternary forms, quaternions, spinor theory). Shares F01, F25, F23.
why: A large catalogue of solved siblings sharing the 'finite explicit exceptions' feature (like U(n)) with documented proof techniques.
first_step: Scan Sun's survey of conjectures on refinements of Lagrange's four-square theorem; list proved ones and their tools.
refs: Z.-W. Sun, Refining Lagrange's four-square theorem, J. Number Theory 175 (2017) 167–190

title: Heath-Brown x³+2y³ cubic parity breaking analogue for norm-form certificates
connection: Heath-Brown's primes of the form x³+2y³ use a Type II estimate on a cubic norm form; ES certificates can be written as divisors of norms from Q(√−d) at fixed p.
why: A norm-form viewpoint replaces 'divisor in residue class' by 'ideal in ray class', where parity-breaking for norm forms exists.
first_step: Write the Type I certificate as: an ideal 𝔞 | (p + 2c√−d) with N𝔞 ≡ −p mod 4cd, i.e. a ray-class condition, and list the ray class field.
refs: Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x^3+2y^3, Acta Math. 186 (2001)

title: S-unit equation finiteness: ES solutions with all denominators S-smooth
connection: If x, y, z, n are all S-units for a fixed finite set S, then 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is an S-unit equation with finitely many non-degenerate solutions (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt).
why: Gives a rigorous negative: no fixed finite set of primes can supply the denominators for infinitely many primes n — a clean barrier for 'smooth-denominator' constructions.
first_step: Write the S-unit equation and its explicit Evertse bound; compare with the data on smoothness of ES denominators at p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt, Linear equations in variables which lie in a multiplicative group, Ann. Math. 155 (2002)
